# Abstract {.unnumbered}

Children increasingly read machine-generated stories on screens, and whether the text properties that govern reading under controlled conditions govern it there is unknown. We will analyse logs from *Let's Story*, a feature of the *Applaydu* app, in which children aged 7 and older read in ten or more languages. We will model reading time per word from lexical difficulty, grammatical load and referential continuity. Six confirmatory hypotheses concern these associations, their moderation by age band, narration's selectivity, children's difficulty ratings and accumulated in-app reading. Bayesian crossed-effects models will represent readings within texts, children and languages. Coefficients outside a region of practical equivalence would support the hypotheses, in either direction for the two that adjudicate between rival developmental accounts, and posteriors inside it would show that the laboratory effects do not transfer. Because families choose narration, texts and continued use, we will report every coefficient as a conditional association.

{{< pagebreak >}}

# Introduction

A generation of children now meets a large share of its reading on a screen, and an increasing share of what appears there was written by a machine. Commercial storytelling applications generate a narrative to order from a handful of choices a family makes, read it aloud in the family's language, and record what the child did with it. The behavioural record such platforms accumulate is far larger than any laboratory corpus of children's reading, spans ten or more languages, and arises under exactly the conditions that laboratory work has to strip away. The count below sizes the evidence base that describes it. We ask whether the text properties that govern reading under controlled conditions still govern it in the wild, and whether their hold on the reader changes over the years in which decoding becomes automatic.

The laboratory answer is well established at three levels of linguistic description. At the level of the word, frequency of occurrence is among the most consistently replicated predictors of reading behaviour that psycholinguistics has produced. High-frequency words are recognised faster and fixated for less time than low-frequency words, and the effect on text reading is closely similar across 12 alphabetic languages [@kupermanWordLengthFrequency2024a]. In children the effect is larger than in adults, reflecting less automatised lexical access [@josephUsingEyeMovements2013]. Frequency norms drawn from subtitle corpora approximate everyday exposure well enough to have become the standard operationalisation [@brysbaertMovingKuceraFrancis2009; @vanheuvenSubtlexUKNewImproved2014]. Resources built from what children actually read, such as the Children and Young People's Books Lexicon, give a still more defensible baseline for developing readers [@korochkinaChildrenYoungPeoples2024]. Related lexical properties behave similarly. Concrete and highly imageable words are processed faster than abstract ones in natural reading [@magnaboscoEyeSemanticsStudy2024] and are remembered better [@paivioDualCodingTheory1991], an advantage usually attributed to the availability of perceptual as well as verbal representations [@bernabeuLanguageSensorimotorSimulation2022; @kaupInterplayModalAmodal2025]. Grounding matters most early in vocabulary development, since the meanings children acquire first are the more concrete ones [@murakiDevelopmentAbstractWord2025]. The diversity of the vocabulary a text deploys is a further index of the demand it places on the reader [@mccarthyMTLDVocdDHDD2010], and vocabulary knowledge constrains comprehension in children more tightly than in skilled adults [@cainReadingComprehensionVocabulary2014].

At the level of the sentence, structure imposes its own cost. Mean dependency distance, the count of embedded clauses and the ratio of subordinate to main clauses all index the demand a text places on the reader to hold a dependent in mind until its head arrives [@gibsonLinguisticComplexityLocality1998]. Long dependencies are expensive because the intervening material has to be carried, and because children's verbal working memory is still developing they are disproportionately affected by that cost relative to adults [@delageSyntaxWorkingMemory2019; @cuiRoleExecutiveFunctions2024; @changInfluencesExecutiveFunction2020]. Syntactic skill is a source of comprehension variance separate from vocabulary in the middle grades [@nielsenSyntacticComprehensionSeparate2025], and sensitivity to grammatical structure continues to underwrite comprehension well past the primary years: Marjokorpi and van Rijt [-@marjokorpiGrammaticalUnderstandingPredicts2025] found explicit grammatical understanding to predict reading comprehension in secondary-school students after socioeconomic background, writing ability and other literacy factors were controlled. The evidence at the grain this study uses is less settled. In the Multilingual Eye-movement Corpus, global measures of syntactic and lexical complexity, including dependency depth and embeddedness, were negligible predictors of adults' sentence and passage reading times once length and position were accounted for [@kupermanGlobalMeasuresSyntactic2025]. Whether a text-level grammatical measure carries a reading-time cost for children reading whole stories is therefore an open question, and Hypothesis 1 is written so that a practically null grammatical coefficient would replicate that adult result in children while a non-negligible one would qualify it.

At the level of the passage, what matters is whether the text states the connection between one idea and the next or leaves the reader to supply it. Sentence-to-sentence semantic similarity, overlap in referring expressions and the density of explicit connectives together index how much of that work the surface of the text has already done [@crossleyToolAutomaticAnalysis2019]. Texts that do more of it are generally easier to follow, and the benefit is largest for readers with least prior knowledge to draw on [@mcnamaraAreGoodTexts1996; @oreillyReversingCohesionEffect2007]. Automated tools now make these indices computable at scale [@graesserCohmetrixMeasuresText2014; @crossleyDevelopingLinguisticConstructs2025], and multi-dimensional characterisations of difficulty built from them outperform the classical readability formulae they replaced [@crossleyAssessingReadabilityFormulas2023; @martincSupervisedUnsupervisedNeural2021; @goldmanReadingComplexImplications2024].

The systematic review that accompanies this protocol sharpens that general account in ways that shape the present design. Text difficulty does not reduce to word frequency: in 924 German fourth-graders, estimated lexical coverage predicted comprehension non-linearly, rising more steeply above roughly 56 per cent coverage [@ludewigVocabularyTextCoverage2023]. In 158 children aged between 8 years 8 months and 11 years 2 months, word frequency, pronoun density, concreteness and deep cohesion each explained unique variance in passage comprehension after decoding and oral language were taken into account, and lexical arousal explained variance beyond them [@pickrenContributionTextCharacteristics2022], which is the direct warrant for carrying affective and discourse variables alongside conventional readability measures. Effects also depend on what is being asked: across 1,229 children in grades 2 to 9, the direction and size of a text characteristic's contribution varied with question type [@aparicioComprehensionPerformancesExplanatory2022]. Feature-based prediction of item-level comprehension from sentence complexity, lexical surprisal and rare-word use is already feasible [@yuyangniePredictingReadingComprehension2022], and syntactic complexity has been shown to impair comprehension accuracy and slow recall in bilingual children [@wasitokiranaSentenceProcessingIndonesianEnglish2025].

Two further strands bear on the present design because they concern the reader and the reading context. The first is the child's history of reading. Longitudinal work consistently shows that this history cannot be read as a simple dose of practice. Using random-intercept cross-lagged models from ages 7 to 16, @torppaLeisureReadingNot2020 found that weaker early reading predicted less subsequent leisure reading, while later within-person increases in book reading predicted gains in comprehension. A ten-year study likewise found reciprocal associations between skill and print exposure, with the skill-to-practice path most visible early and accumulated exposure becoming more predictive later [@vanbergenHowArePractice2021]. Accumulated use of an app therefore carries both practice and the stable differences in skill and motivation that produced the use in the first place, so we will estimate within-child change and between-child differences separately.

The second is narration. Read-aloud audio is often treated as a uniform benefit, and the evidence does not support that reading. A meta-analysis of 30 reading-while-listening studies (62 effects, total *N* = 1,945) found a small pooled comprehension advantage ($g$ = 0.18), no reliable advantage where ordinary reading was self-paced ($g$ = 0.06, 95 per cent CI [-0.07, 0.19]), and a larger one only where ordinary reading was paced by the experimenter ($g$ = 0.41, 95 per cent CI [0.13, 0.70]) [@clintonlisellDoesReadingWhile2023]. Among students with reading difficulties, text-to-speech tools showed a moderate pooled effect ($d$ = 0.35) that fell to $d$ = 0.15 and included zero in within-participant designs [@woodUseTexttoSpeech2018]. Neither synthesis settles the mechanism, which a large naturalistic corpus is well placed to address. If a spoken rendition works by supplying word identity without print-to-sound mapping, it should remove much of the cost that lexical difficulty imposes while leaving the cost of connecting ideas largely intact. If narrated reading time is instead set by the duration of the recording, every text property should lose its purchase on time in the same proportion. Hypothesis 4 is written to separate these accounts.

The size of the relevant literature can be counted. On 26 August 2026, a Scopus search over 2018 to 2026 returned 3,701 records on children's reading comprehension, 6,592 on computational text features and 133,132 on platform log data. The pairwise intersections were 17, 28 and 45 records, and the three-way intersection was empty. The exact expressions are reproduced in the supplementary search record, the script that issues them and archives their counts is deposited with this protocol [@bernabeuScopusflow2026], and @fig-gap shows the sets. Over the same window, records combining children's reading with machine-generated text went from none before 2024 to two, six and four in the three years since. That small strand consists of classroom experiments: 106 Turkish fourth-graders who read stories generated from their own prompts gained in comprehension and motivation over controls [@balantekinImprovingStudentsReading2026], and a further trial reports similar gains for generated science stories [@bulutImpactAISTEMBased2026]. These studies measure outcomes in the classroom and describe the texts qualitatively. The laboratory counterpart for adults is recent: a corpus of eye movements from 107 English-speaking adults reading machine-generated texts of six kinds, annotated with the generating models' internals [@bolligerEMTeCCorpusEye2025].

*Let's Story*, a feature of the *Applaydu* app developed by Gameloft and Ferrero International, combines the three topics of that count. Families choose a setting, a hero, a companion, a plot and a theme, the five story attributes the platform's data dictionary records for each generated story. A generative model then writes a narrative around those choices, and the app renders it as an illustrated storybook and, at the family's option, reads it aloud [@ratnerDidRobotWrite2025]. Every completed reading is logged, with the time taken, the language, the child's age band, the reading level the family has set and an optional judgement of how hard the story was. Comparable platforms have been studied one feature at a time. @bootonImpactMobileApplication2023 reviewed 11 studies and found inbuilt narration to aid comprehension and word learning, while text-linked interactive hotspots showed no evidence of benefit. Content analyses of the wider market are less encouraging: @furlongFindingNeedleHaystack2025 found expert reviewers willing to recommend only 27.5 per cent of 309 phonics apps, with consumer star ratings a poor guide to expert quality, and @chatzopoulosEvaluationGooglePlay2023 found educational content to be the dimension in which the largest share of 50 Google Play apps scored poorly. Log data from a research-oriented platform have been shown to track ability, with reading speed in the BookBites app correlating with standardised scores at *r* = .39 to .48 [@sortkaerBothSidesStory2021]. The commercial edutainment sector, whose user base is far larger, has been studied through content analyses and small experiments rather than through its logs.

The theoretical commitments behind the hypotheses are held in a machine-checkable theory object, deposited with this protocol, that names twelve constructs, eighteen propositions each carrying the mechanism it claims, six auxiliary assumptions and six rival accounts, and records which prediction is derived from which proposition and which rival it is meant to separate. @fig-net is generated from that object, so the figure and the hypotheses cannot drift apart on the counts, scores and derivation links the checks enforce. The object passes all twelve items of the versioned rigour checklist implemented in theoryforge, scoring 90.9 out of 100 (Supplementary Section S1) [@bernabeuTheoryforge2026]. Its causal graph is acyclic, so implications can be derived from it mechanically: that the three text properties are mutually independent given the reading level and the generation route, that narration is unrelated to accumulated reading, and that the difficulty rating adds nothing about reading level once reading time is known. We will test these implications before interpreting the confirmatory models, against the criterion registered under Outcome-neutral quality checks, and we will report any failure.

This study is observational throughout. Children choose their stories, their reading level and whether to switch narration on, and families choose whether to keep using the app. A protocol built on such records has to say what that gains and what it costs, because platform data answer a different question from an experiment. A laboratory experiment establishes that a text property *can* move reading when an experimenter controls the text, the setting and the task. It cannot establish that the property *does* move reading when nobody controls anything. The second question is one about generalisation, and it cannot be settled in the setting that produced the original result [@yarkoniGeneralizabilityCrisis2022; @nastaseKeepItReal2020]. Explanation and prediction are best treated as complementary aims served by different designs [@hofmanPredictionExplanationSocial2017; @hofmanIntegratingExplanationPrediction2021], and the same holds for control and representativeness. Mining naturally occurring records is by now an established methodology with its own accumulated cautions [@goldstoneDiscoveringPsychologicalPrinciples2016; @paxtonFindingTracesBehavioral2017], and the account below draws on them.

The platform's first advantage is stimulus sampling. Reading research has known since Clark [-@clarkLanguageasfixedeffectFallacy1973] that treating a handful of experimenter-written texts as a fixed set inflates confidence in conclusions meant to hold for texts in general, and the mixed-model solution has been available for over a decade [@juddTreatingStimuliRandom2012]. Yarkoni's [-@yarkoniGeneralizabilityCrisis2022] survey of the problem found that psychologists routinely model variation between participants while leaving stimuli, tasks and sites unmodelled, which constrains generalisation far more tightly than most reports acknowledge. The design here treats Text as a crossed random factor over hundreds of texts that children selected for themselves, which is both the prescribed remedy and, in Brunswik's sense, a representative design: the stimuli are sampled from the environment the reader inhabits, where a systematic design would construct them to instantiate a factorial contrast [@dhamiRoleRepresentativeDesign2004]. We avoid the phrase *ecological validity* throughout, since it has been shown to carry several incompatible meanings in current use [@hollemanRealWorldApproachIts2020; @kihlstromEcologicalValidityEcological2021]. The claim made here is the narrower and checkable one about how the stimuli were sampled. The precision analysis makes the same point in reverse, since every text coefficient is bounded by how many distinct texts there are, however many sessions the extract holds.

Linguistic breadth is the second gain. English dominates cognitive science to a degree that warps which mechanisms are studied and licenses overgeneralisation from one atypical language to the species [@blasiOverrelianceEnglishHinders2022]. Reading is among the worst affected, because writing systems differ in ways that matter for every stage of processing. The most ambitious response to date, the Multilingual Eye-movement Corpus, assembled eye-tracking during text reading in 13 languages in its first wave through an international multi-laboratory collaboration, and its authors open by reporting that the existing empirical base is insufficient for cross-linguistic comparison [@siegelmanExpandingHorizonsCrosslinguistic2022]. A second wave has since extended it to 21 languages, adding logographic and abugida writing systems [@siegelmanWave2Multilingual2025]. A commercial platform reaches many of the same languages incidentally, in far larger numbers of readers per language, and reaches children where the corpus records skilled adults. The comparison must be stated precisely, because MECO records eye movements and this study records only whole-story duration. The platform gains breadth and loses resolution, and a given question needs one or the other.

The third gain is behaviour as it occurred. Where the alternative measure of how much or how fast a child reads is an adult's recollection, the log is the better instrument: logged and self-reported digital media use diverge systematically enough to have warranted a meta-analysis of the discrepancy [@parrySystematicReviewMetaanalysis2021], and in 109 French primary-school children parents' estimates of weekly reading time were three times the logged figure, which predicted fluency better [@brossetteMeasuringReadingTime2026].

Against this stands the strongest statistical objection to any large non-random dataset. Meng's [-@mengStatisticalParadisesParadoxes2018] decomposition shows that the error of a sample mean is the product of three quantities. One indexes data quality, as the correlation between the recorded value and whether it was recorded at all. The other two index data quantity and the difficulty of the problem. Probability sampling holds the first near zero. Once it is not held there, the population size stops cancelling: for any given sample size, estimation error then grows with the square root of the population. Bradley and colleagues [-@bradleyUnrepresentativeBigSurveys2021] gave the canonical demonstration: two surveys collecting roughly 250,000 responses a week and 75,000 a fortnight overestimated United States COVID-19 vaccine uptake by 17 and 14 percentage points, with margins of error so small that the wrong answers looked precise, while a well-designed panel of about 1,000 responses a week was accurate. Scale converts a small bias into a confident error, and it did so at Google before it did so in the pandemic [@lazerParableGoogleFlu2014]. Every selection gate in this study is a candidate for that correlation: who owns a tablet, who installs an app tied to a confectionery brand, who registers consent for research use, who switches narration off, and who finishes a story.

That objection is real, and it also has a boundary, which must be drawn accurately. Meng's result concerns the estimation of a population mean, and this study estimates no population mean. Its estimands are conditional associations inside the sample, such as the change in log reading time per word for a one-standard-deviation change in lexical difficulty, within a language and within a reading level. A sample that is unrepresentative in who it contains biases such a slope only when selection depends on the outcome given the predictors, which is a narrower condition than the one that wrecks a mean. The consequence falls on the claim: we will report these coefficients as estimates for children who read on this platform, and we will not present them as population values for children in general, nor will we report a population mean of reading speed for any group.

One selection gate does meet the narrower condition, and it deserves separate treatment. The extract contains completed readings only, so the analysis conditions on completion, which is plausibly a common effect of the text's difficulty and the reader's capacity. Conditioning on a common effect can induce an association between its causes where none existed [@rohrerThinkingClearlyCorrelations2018]. The direction here is predictable: if harder texts are abandoned more often, the hard texts that survive into the data are disproportionately those read by children who could manage them, which attenuates the very coefficients Hypothesis 1 predicts. The bias therefore works against our own prediction, so a non-negligible result survives the objection more comfortably than a null does, and the practical consequence is that an inside-region verdict for Hypotheses 1 to 3 must be reported with the completion rate beside it. That rate is question (k) to the data controller.

Nothing here is randomised, and we do not use causal verbs for variables that families chose. That restraint is not the same as pretending the questions are not causal: euphemism has been argued to damage observational research by obscuring what is actually being asked [@hernanCWordScientificEuphemisms2018; @groszTabooAgainstExplicit2020]. We state the causal structure explicitly in a deposited graph, derive the adjustment set from it, register the rival explanations it implies, and then report associations conditional on that adjustment. Estimating the text coefficients within reading level, for instance, is a consequence of the graph, and the graph itself entails it.

Secondary data also invite the analytic flexibility that preregistration exists to remove, and the field has developed specific standards for preregistering analyses of data that already exist [@westonRecommendationsIncreasingTransparency2019; @vandenakkerPreregistrationSecondaryData2021]. The arrangement described under Data provenance goes further on the point that matters most. The extract is unanalysed because it is absent. The data controller holds it, and it reaches us only after in-principle acceptance, so the most common objection to observational work, that the analyst saw the data before choosing the analysis, does not arise.

When 160 teams applied machine learning to a rich birth-cohort dataset to predict six life outcomes, the best predictions were barely better than a simple benchmark [@salganikMeasuringPredictabilityLife2020]. This study accordingly makes a narrow claim. It does not attempt to predict a child's reading, but to estimate a handful of pre-specified associations whose attainable precision we calculated before the data were released, and to say in advance which of them the available records cannot settle. A last limit applies to any aggregate: group-level associations need not describe any individual, and variance around an expected value has been found to be two to four times larger within people than within groups [@fisherLackGrouptoindividualGeneralizability2018]. This is why tier 2 separates each child's own change from the differences between children, and why the two are never reported as a single quantity.

Three consequences of all this are built into the design. First, the reading level a family sets determines which version of a text the platform serves, so text difficulty is partly assigned by a choice that also reflects the child's capacity, and we will therefore estimate the text coefficients within reading level and check whether they survive that restriction. Second, the app records elapsed time for a whole story and never for a page, so the outcome is a rate, and we state below which analyses that forecloses. Third, the data carry no measure of any individual child's reading skill, vocabulary or language background, so age band stands in for a bundle of developing capacities and is interpreted as nothing finer.

Six confirmatory hypotheses follow, set out with their sampling and analysis plans, the precision each test requires and the reading of every possible outcome in @tbl-design. Two of them, the interactions between the text properties and the age band, are registered as two-sided tests that adjudicate between rival accounts, because the direct developmental evidence in this age range supports neither sign. Three text components carry the confirmatory predictions. LexicalDifficulty and GrammaticalLoad are oriented so that higher scores mean a more demanding text, and ReferentialContinuity so that higher scores mean a text that states more of the links between its ideas. Signs are fixed before any component score is joined to an outcome. The age band and narration enter the models as deviations from their observed prevalence: a reading scores 1 for the older band, or for narration on, and 0 otherwise, minus the proportion of tier-1 readings in that state. Each component's main effect is then its prevalence-weighted average slope across the two states, which carries no design effect from imbalance, and each interaction is the difference in slope between the two states, positive when the slope is larger in the older band or under narration. The outcome for Hypotheses 1 to 4 and 6 is log reading time per word, standardised within language, so a coefficient is a within-language standardised slope and the region of practical equivalence is 0.05 standard deviations. Hypothesis 4 concerns a difference between two attenuation proportions, with a region of 0.05 on that difference. Hypothesis 5 uses the child's own three-point difficulty rating on an ordinal scale, where the region is a half-width of log(1.05) on the log-odds scale, an odds ratio between 0.952 and 1.05.

Because the two main effects run in opposite directions, the same developmental claim takes opposite signs in the two interaction terms. Grammatical load is associated with slower reading, so a weaker association in older children makes a positive slope smaller and the interaction negative. Referential continuity is associated with faster reading, so a weaker association in older children makes a negative slope less negative and the interaction positive. Wherever an account is described below as predicting that a text property bears less on the older reader, the sign of the corresponding coefficient follows from this convention alone.

The outcome is the logarithm of reading time, for a reason the hypotheses depend on. Children in the two age bands differ in overall reading rate, and a difference in rate that is purely multiplicative manufactures a spurious interaction on a raw time scale [@faustIndividualDifferencesInformation1999]. On the log scale a multiplicative difference in rate appears as a main effect and never as an interaction, so every interaction reported here is a difference in *proportional* cost. A second feature of the outcome is fixed for a related reason. In the standard cohesion manipulation the more cohesive version of a text is 20 to 40 per cent longer, so a duration aggregated over a whole text would show higher coherence slowing reading for arithmetic reasons alone. Dividing by word count and retaining log text length as a covariate closes that path, and a raw duration is never used as an outcome.

@tbl-design sets out each hypothesis against the sampling and analysis plan that tests it, the precision the design analysis says that test requires, how each possible outcome will be read, and what would be shown wrong. We fixed every row before any outcome data existed.

More than 95 per cent below -0.05 is reverse selectivity, contradicts both accounts and is reported as such. Anything else is inconclusive and both accounts remain live. If the gate fails, H4 is reported as not evaluable. If the compression diagnostic fires, the full-sample verdict is withheld and H4 rests on the unpaced subset. Shown wrong: either the decoding-scaffolding account of narration or the audio-pacing account; the contrast is constructed so that they cannot both survive. |
| Do children's own difficulty judgements track the same text properties? | H5. LexicalDifficulty and GrammaticalLoad are associated with higher odds, and ReferentialContinuity with lower odds, of a harder rating, each outside the region, and the three rank by magnitude as in the reading-time model. | Tier-1 sessions carrying a rating. A text rated by fewer than five distinct children does not contribute. The primary model is complete-case, with an inverse-probability sensitivity analysis for non-response. ROPE of a half-width of log(1.05) on the log-odds scale. At the 30 per cent availability the structural sample showed, the 0.90 target is not reached within the 1,600 texts simulated and projects to roughly 8,000 to 8,700 generated texts, about 2,300 to 2,500 carrying at least five ratings (Supplementary Section S5). The simulation will be re-run at the observed availability before fitting. This is the hypothesis most likely to be declared underpowered. | Ordinal cumulative-logit model with the same fixed and grouping structure and language-varying thresholds. The ordering claim is the posterior probability that the three coefficients rank by magnitude as they do for reading time, read against the 0.90 criterion registered under Decision rules. | All three odds ratios outside the region in the predicted directions and ordering probability at least 0.90: two independent measurements converge on the same ordering of text demands. Odds ratios in the predicted directions but ordering probability below 0.90: partial convergence; the rating is usable as a difficulty signal but not as a rank measure. Odds ratios inside the region while the reading-time coefficients are non-negligible: the rating is not a usable measure of experienced difficulty, and the ordering is not interpreted. Both outcomes null: the components themselves are suspect. If underpowered, the ordering is reported descriptively and convergent validity is recorded as not established. Shown wrong: that reading time and reported difficulty are both readouts of the same expended effort. |
| Within a child, is more accumulated in-app reading associated with a faster pace? | H6. Within a child, accumulated in-app reading is negatively associated with log time per word. | Tier 2: children with at least three eligible sessions on distinct texts. The simulated requirement is 563 children (463 to 674) at five readings each for 0.90 and 681 (543 to 834) for 0.95, for the unadjusted trend; the tier-2 sweep will be re-run at the observed sessions-per-child distribution with the registered covariates added, and the hypothesis is declared underpowered, not untestable, below the re-run threshold. | The tier-1 specification refitted on tier 2 with a child varying intercept, decomposing accumulated words into the child's mean and the session's deviation from it, alongside session order, days since the previous session and days since the child's first eligible session. The deviation term is the registered test. | Negative and outside the ROPE: an association over the observation window, never a practice effect, because skill and practice are reciprocal over longer spans and maturation is the named residual alternative. Positive and outside: contradicts the consolidation account and is read as within-window slowing that the covariates do not capture. Inside the ROPE: evidence against a within-window consolidation signal of at least 0.05 *SD*. Shown wrong: that reading consolidates the recognition machinery reading depends on, within a window short enough for the reverse path to be unlikely to dominate. |

: Study design table. Eligibility for every row: sessions the platform flags as incomplete, crashed or duplicated, and accounts flagged as duplicates under the platform's own rules, are removed; a story needs a positive word count; a reading faster than 400 or slower than 10 words per minute is excluded; only an account's first reading of a text enters tier 1; and readings sharing a session-timeout value are treated as right-censored where the registered rule triggers. No datum is ever replaced. {#tbl-design tbl-colwidths="[13,17,24,22,24]"}

*Hypothesis 1: text properties and reading pace.* We predict that, across distinct texts and within reading level and language, LexicalDifficulty and GrammaticalLoad will each show a positive association with log reading time per word, and ReferentialContinuity a negative one. The three coefficients are evaluated and labelled separately, and the failure of one does not suppress reporting of the others. An overall verdict on Hypothesis 1 is recorded only when all three are practically non-negligible in the predicted direction. A coefficient that is practically non-negligible in the opposite direction is read as evidence against the corresponding proposition of the theory object, and a positive continuity coefficient in particular as a whole-text reverse cohesion effect of the kind reported for high-knowledge readers [@mcnamaraAreGoodTexts1996; @oreillyReversingCohesionEffect2007]. Such a coefficient blocks the combined verdict without suppressing the others. A coefficient practically equivalent to zero is evidence that the property's laboratory effect does not reach 0.05 standard deviations in this setting, which for the grammatical component would extend to children the negligible passage-level effect of global complexity measures reported for adults [@kupermanGlobalMeasuresSyntactic2025].

*Hypothesis 2: grammatical load and the age band.* We register the GrammaticalLoad × AgeBand interaction as a two-sided adjudicating test, because two accounts of what changes between these ages predict opposite signs on the scale this study uses. On the capacity account, a grammatical dependency costs time in proportion to how close its maintenance comes to exhausting the working memory available, so as that capacity matures the same structure costs proportionally less and the interaction is negative [@delageSyntaxWorkingMemory2019; @pengExaminingMediationEffects2018]. On the experience account, what changes is exposure: an older reader has met complex structure far more often and has been taught the punctuation that marks its boundaries, engages with it more fully in consequence, and pays a proportionally larger cost, which makes the interaction positive [@macdonaldReassessingWorkingMemory2002; @montagInfluenceLanguageStatistics2015].

The direct evidence does not decide between the accounts. The largest eye-movement sample over this band, 81 children reading 12 items, found no attenuation at all, but it manipulated temporary ambiguity, which indexes reanalysis and not the sustained maintenance that dependency length imposes, so its null does not transfer to the present operationalisation [@wonnacottChildrensReadingGood2016]. Where an interaction has been reported it was confined to late measures with fourteen children per group [@josephChildrensAdultsOnline2013]. That study's tables let the effect be expressed as a proportion of baseline, and the two measures disagree. On go-past time in the target region, our computation gives 15 per cent in the younger children, 25 per cent in the older and 31 per cent in adults, which is the pattern a positive interaction would reproduce on a proportional scale. On post-target total reading time, where the study's own significant interaction lay, the proportional effect ran the other way, from 27 per cent in the younger children to 12 per cent in the older and 4.5 per cent in adults. A third possibility is that development over this band is not monotonic at all: the largest of the existing tests, with 250 children aged 8 to 11, found the processing of complex sentences to change unevenly across that range [@boothDevelopmentRelativeClause2000]. A negative interaction outside the region of practical equivalence supports the capacity account, a positive one supports the experience account, and a posterior lying inside the region is evidence that neither developmental signature reaches a detectable size across these two bands. That third outcome carries a caveat: a non-monotonic trajectory cancelling across two coarse bands would produce the same posterior, which is why the ordinal-age sensitivity analysis is registered under Sensitivity analyses. It would still be informative, since the existing tests of this interaction range from 14 children per group to 250, and the eye-movement tests to 81.

*Hypothesis 3: referential continuity and the age band.* We register the ReferentialContinuity × AgeBand interaction the same way, because the construction-integration framework supplies two moderators of coherence facilitation that both rise between 7 and 11 and push in opposite directions. On the knowledge account, a reader who cannot bridge a gap from what they already know depends on the text to state the connection, so surface continuity is worth most to the younger reader and the interaction is positive, the facilitation being a negative slope that becomes less negative with age. On the cue-utilisation account, exploiting a connective requires enough decoding fluency to reach it and enough explicit knowledge of what it signals, so the older reader gains more and the interaction is negative. The clearest evidence that strategic, high-knowledge readers gain from cohesion comes from undergraduates [@oreillyReversingCohesionEffect2007].

Here too the existing evidence does not decide between the accounts. Eight- and ten-year-olds gained the same speed-up from an appropriate connective in self-paced reading, with the age interaction explicitly null across 91 children [@cainInfluenceConnectivesYoung2011]. Online sensitivity to a coherence break did not differ between children of 8 to 9 and children of 10 to 11 [@helderCoherenceMonitoringGood2016]. In the demonstration of a reverse cohesion effect in fourth-graders, the effect of cohesion turned on world knowledge and depended far less on decoding skill, with age untestable within a single grade [@mcnamaraComprehensionChallengesFourth2011]. Reading rate under a whole-text coherence manipulation has, to our knowledge, not been measured in this age range. The three outcomes are read as for Hypothesis 2. Because the sign of a coherence effect also depends on which cohesive device carries it, connectives enter by relation type and the component's anchors are the causal and contrastive connectives, for the reason given under the dimension reduction.

*Hypothesis 4: the selectivity of narration.* We predict that the LexicalDifficulty coefficient will be proportionally smaller under narration than the ReferentialContinuity coefficient is. Writing $\pi_{\text{lex}}$ and $\pi_{\text{cont}}$ for the proportional attenuation of each coefficient under narration, computed draw by draw from the posterior under the rule given under Confirmatory models, the prediction is that $\pi_{\text{lex}} - \pi_{\text{cont}} > 0.20$. A spoken rendition supplies word identity without print-to-sound mapping, which is the step that a low-frequency or long word makes expensive, and it does not supply the link between two ideas, which the reader must still construct. Reading aloud the directions, proper nouns and questions of a test while the child still decodes the passages helps poor decoders with adequate listening comprehension, and pacing alone did not produce the gain [@giustoReadAloudAccommodation2019]. The benefit of text-to-speech is largest for children whose decoding is weak but whose language is intact [@keelorImpactTexttospeechFeatures2023], and within a narrated passage the time saved falls on the first encounter with an orthographically novel word and has gone by the second [@valentiniReadingWhileListening2024].

The competing account holds that narrated reading time is set by the duration of the recording, in which case every text coefficient shrinks by the same proportion and $\pi_{\text{lex}} - \pi_{\text{cont}} = 0$. That account has substantial support of its own. The aggregate comprehension benefit of reading while listening is confined to studies whose comparison condition was externally paced [@clintonlisellDoesReadingWhile2023; @clintonlisellReadingVersusListening2022]. A preregistered test of the resource-freeing mechanism in adult second-language readers found comprehension *worse* under narration than in silent reading [@huiForcedPaceReading2026]. Where the compression has been measured incidentally it is severe: the standard deviation of exposure time fell from 11.56 seconds when self-paced to 0.62 seconds when narrated [@valentiniReadingWhileListening2024]. Neither account has been tested on the contrast that would separate them, which is reading time regressed on decoding-level and on integration-level text predictors separately, in narrated and unnarrated reading of the same texts.

Four outcomes are registered, with the posterior criteria given under Decision rules. A difference above 0.20 supports selective removal of decoding cost. A difference practically equivalent to zero supports the account on which the recording sets the pace. A difference determinately below -0.05, meaning that narration removes more of the continuity cost than of the lexical cost, is reverse selectivity, which contradicts both accounts and will be reported as such. Anything else is inconclusive and both accounts remain live. The threshold of 0.20 is four times the region's half-width and is a registered convention.

Who reads without narration is itself a selection. Narration was on in about nine sessions in ten of the structural sample, so the unnarrated slopes, which are the denominators of both attenuation proportions, are estimated largely from the families who chose to switch the audio off. If those are disproportionately the fluent readers, their slopes are attenuated by selection and both proportions are distorted, and the data carry no measure of reading skill with which to adjust for this. We will therefore report narration prevalence by age band, reading level and language before fitting, and the rule under Confirmatory models promotes the within-account contrast to the primary estimate where the data allow it. Two further guards, a registered compression diagnostic and a repeat of the contrast in the narrated sessions the audio cannot have paced, are specified there as well. Because the contrast is a ratio, it is evaluated only when the unnarrated slopes of the lexical and continuity components are both practically non-negligible. If either is not, there is no attenuation to compare and Hypothesis 4 is reported as not evaluable. This gating rule does not depend on the sign of any coefficient.

*Hypothesis 5: the child's own judgement of difficulty.* We predict that, in an ordinal model of the post-reading rating, LexicalDifficulty and GrammaticalLoad will be associated with higher odds of a harder rating and ReferentialContinuity with lower odds, each by an odds ratio outside the region, and that the three standardised coefficients will rank by magnitude as they do in the reading-time model. The second clause makes this more than Hypothesis 1 repeated on a second outcome. Two measures of the same three constructs, one behavioural and one introspective, obtained on different scales from overlapping sets of children, should rank those constructs the same way, and we will report the posterior probability that they do as the study's principal convergent-validity check. That probability is read against a registered criterion: at least 0.90 counts as agreement on order, and anything lower counts as order not established.

Two facts about the rating constrain the design, and neither is established in the literature. To our knowledge, no published study has had children of this age give a global post-reading judgement of how difficult a text was and validated it against the text's measured properties: the child metacognition literature rates adjacent things, such as confidence in one's own answers, judgements of learning for word lists and enjoyment of an activity. The three-point easy, just right and difficult format is a classroom heuristic with no published psychometric validation, and nothing licenses assuming that a single rating from a single child is reliable. That children can validly judge text difficulty is therefore something this study tests, and not something it assumes.

For the design, the effective sample size is the number of distinct children rating each text, and the raw count of ratings overstates it, so the model carries a text varying intercept, and we will report the distribution of raters per text before fitting, applying the five-rater floor registered under Confirmatory models. We will report the intraclass correlation for the rating at text level, a reliability estimate for this format.

For interpretation, a failure here is ambiguous on its own, and Hypothesis 1 resolves it. If the text components predict reading time but their odds ratios for the rating lie inside the region, the feature pipeline is sound and the rating is not a usable measure of experienced difficulty, which is worth reporting given how widely such single-item checks are deployed in educational software, and the ordering is then not interpreted. If the odds ratios lie outside the region in the predicted directions but the ordering probability falls below 0.90, the convergence is partial, and the rating is usable as a difficulty signal though not as a rank measure. If the components predict neither outcome, the components themselves are suspect. If they predict both and in the same order, two independent measurements converge on the same ordering of text demands. All four readings are recorded here in advance. This hypothesis is also the one the design analysis marks as most likely to be underpowered. An inconclusive verdict at the census is itself informative, because it bounds the reliability a single-item difficulty check can have at the availability such apps achieve. In that case the ordering is reported descriptively and convergent validity is recorded as not established, so that the fifth outcome-neutral check has a defined outcome whether or not Hypothesis 5 reaches a verdict.

*Hypothesis 6: accumulated reading and pace.* We predict that, among children with several recorded sessions, a doubling of a child's own accumulated in-app reading will be followed by a reduction in that child's log reading time per word, over and above session order, the interval since the previous session and the time elapsed since the child's first session. On the consolidation account, every encounter with a written word form sharpens the representation supporting its later recognition, so reading consolidates the machinery that makes reading cheap. The relation between practice and skill is reciprocal over years [@torppaLeisureReadingNot2020; @vanbergenHowArePractice2021], so the coefficient is an association within the observation window, and never an estimate of a practice effect. Ordinary maturation over a months-long window would also make a child faster, and accumulated words rise with elapsed time within every child. The elapsed-time covariate is what separates the two, and maturation remains the named residual alternative wherever the coefficient is reported. A positive within-child coefficient outside the region contradicts the consolidation account and is read as within-window slowing that the covariates do not capture. A posterior inside the region is evidence against a within-window consolidation signal of at least 0.05 standard deviations. This hypothesis depends on a subsample whose size is not known before the extract is released, and it is declared underpowered, not untestable, if that subsample falls below the threshold re-derived for it under Design and precision analysis.

Every hypothesis is labelled under the single posterior rule given under Decision rules and diagnostics, and an inconclusive result is reported as such. No hypothesis is filtered by a preliminary significance test. Three labels apply before a verdict. A hypothesis is declared untestable, before its model is fitted and without reference to any coefficient, if its component fails the construction rule set out under the dimension reduction or if its outcome or contrast is absent from the frozen extract. A hypothesis whose data fall below the precision threshold recorded for it in @tbl-design, as re-derived under Design and precision analysis where that section says so, is instead declared underpowered: its model is still fitted and reported, and no conclusion is drawn from an interval the design analysis predicted would be indeterminate. A hypothesis is reported as not evaluable when a registered post-fitting contingency removes its test, which happens in two cases only: the Hypothesis 4 gate, and failure of the positive control on the timing column.

The limits of what follows should be equally clear. This study will not identify a causal effect of any text property, age band or narration setting. It will not estimate how fast children in general read, nor generalise beyond families who chose to install and use this application. It will say nothing about comprehension, since none of the contingent hypotheses is activated at submission. Where the data controller's answers falsify an auxiliary assumption, the affected predictions are reassigned by the rules in @tbl-unresolved, never reinterpreted after the fact.
