# Methods

## Ethics information

This research complies with all relevant ethical regulations. Data are generated in the ordinary operation of a commercial application and are collected by its publisher under the terms of use and privacy policy a family accepts on installation, with consent for research use of anonymised records registered in the app by a parent or guardian. That registration is the informed consent under which the records reach us, and no further consent is sought because no participant is contacted. We play no part in collection, have no contact of any kind with any child or family, and return nothing to the platform, so nothing done here can alter what any child experiences. No compensation is provided or applicable, because the records arise from families' ordinary use of the app. The extract supplied to us carries no direct identifier: the account key is a pseudonymous string generated by the platform, and no name, contact detail, precise location or device identifier is included. Ethical approval for secondary analysis of these anonymised records [has been granted by / is being sought from] the Departmental Research Ethics Committee of the Department of Education, University of Oxford (reference [to be inserted]), and will be in place before acceptance in principle. The study involves no experimental manipulation and no intervention, so it raises no question of withdrawal from a procedure. A family's right to have its records erased is exercised through the platform, and any erasure occurring between the building of the extract and its transfer will be recorded by the data controller and reported at Stage 2.

Two conventions hold throughout this section. First, no decision about whether a hypothesis is tested, on which sample it is tested, or with which model, depends on a fitted coefficient: every such decision is a function of provider-computed counts, of written answers from the data controller, or of thresholds registered here, with one exception, the Hypothesis 4 gate. Four registered contingencies read fitted quantities after fitting and are listed under Decision rules and diagnostics. Second, wherever the text says a quantity will be reported, we will report it in the Stage 2 manuscript whether or not it changes a conclusion.

## Pilot data

The pilot material is a 35-row structural sample of the session table, the data dictionary, and a summary of that sample computed with the count script described under Data provenance. The first two were received from the data controller on 27 July 2026 to confirm the shape of the table, and the third we computed from the sample on 6 August 2026. The sample carries real reading times for 35 sessions on five distinct texts, one session per account, in ten reading languages. It cannot support any hypothesis in this protocol: none is identified by 35 observations, and every within-child term requires accounts with more than one session, of which it contains none. It fixed three inputs of the design analysis, which are the narration prevalence (on in 32 of 35 sessions), the rating availability (present in 10 of 35) and the age-band missingness (blank in 10 of 35), and Supplementary Section S8 reports it in full. The sample is deposited for peer review under embargo until Stage 2 acceptance, at the location the Data availability statement names.

## Design

### Data provenance, sequestration and outcome blindness

The data this protocol analyses already exist. Nature Human Behaviour admits secondary analyses of existing data on condition that authors can evidence no prior access to the data in question. We put the arrangement set out below to the journal's editorial office, which confirmed it as appropriate on 3 August 2026, before we wrote this protocol.

The data controller builds the export now, on its own release cycle, and holds it. Nothing of the session-level file reaches us until the journal confirms in-principle acceptance in writing. In the interval, three things may pass to us, each of which the editorial office agreed may be received in advance. The first is a manifest: the column list, the row count, the cut-off timestamp, the build date and a SHA-256 checksum for every file, so that the file eventually transferred can be shown to be the file that was built. The second is the story texts, keyed by story identifier, reading language, reading level and app version, with page breaks preserved, because every linguistic measure in this protocol is computed on them and none of them contains a behavioural outcome. The third is a set of aggregate counts computed by the data controller from the export by running a script we supplied, which reads nineteen categorical columns and the reading-time column, writes one small table of counts and a page drawn from it, and never reports a reading time as a value. At submission we hold the story texts, received on [date]. The manifest and the provider-computed counts [had been received on DATE / had not yet been received], and the count of distinct texts with eligible readings in the extract, which only those counts settle, is reported in @tbl-unresolved as unresolved: the texts we hold are keyed by identifier, language, reading level and app version, but which of them carry eligible readings, and how many readings each carries, is a fact about the extract and not about the texts.

The counts are described in detail because a count computed from an outcome column is where blindness would fail. The script treats reading time only as a column whose usability has to be established. It reports how many values are absent, non-numeric, negative or zero, and how many fall into each of seven bands whose boundaries are successive powers of ten, together with the number of distinct values the column holds and the largest number of sessions sharing any single value. It never crosses reading time with language, age, text, account or date. Bands ten times wider than one another cannot distinguish a fast text from a slow one. What they can distinguish is a column recorded in seconds from one recorded in milliseconds, which the analysis has to know before it can be specified at all. The count of sessions sharing one value is how a session-timeout cap makes itself visible, and the sampling plan below turns that count into a registered decision about censoring.

The structural sample and the summary computed on it, described under Pilot data, are part of the record. At the editorial office's specific direction, we have not run the dimension reduction specified below and will not run it before submission, although we hold the texts on which it would operate. The component solution is therefore fully specified here and entirely unfitted.

The data controller will supply a signed certification naming an owner and a deputy for the held file, and stating its build date, its window, its row count and its checksums. The same document certifies three things about what has happened to the file. It certifies that the file has not been transferred in whole or in part to the research team or to anyone acting for it. It certifies that the file will be transferred only on written confirmation of in-principle acceptance. And it certifies that no analysis relating story text to reading time has been conducted by the controller or reported to the team. It is reproduced in the supplementary material.

### Materials

The reading materials are the story texts themselves. A family chooses a setting, a hero, a companion, a plot and a theme, and a generative model writes a narrative around that combination. The text is then fixed, and it is not rewritten when the same combination is chosen again. Texts also exist in a fixed classic set that families may read instead of a generated story. Alongside the texts, the extract records which of the two a reading drew on, the reading level the platform was serving, the language, the app version and the page count. Every session will be joined to the features of the exact version it was served, matched on story identifier, reading language, reading level and app version, so no model uses features computed on a version of a text the child did not see.

For identification, a text is a stimulus shared by many readers, and every text coefficient in this protocol is identified by comparing texts. How many distinct texts carry eligible readings is therefore the single quantity that governs how much this design can establish, and it is not yet known. The data controller's own estimate spans a few hundred to a few million, according to whether one combination of chosen attributes maps to one text shared by everyone who picks it or to a separate text per session. The published description of the platform before launch is the prior on both questions: a catalogue of over 40,000 English-language stories generated from the element combinations, many of them translated into the child's home language [@ratnerDidRobotWrite2025]. If that description holds for the window, texts are shared across sessions and differ across languages by translation, which would trigger the varying intercept for the underlying story crossed with Language that @tbl-unresolved registers under question (d). The controller's written answer supersedes it. The design analysis below is built around that uncertainty, and @tbl-unresolved records what follows from each answer.

For every text, we will compute features in four families. *Lexical* features are mean log frequency of content words, the proportion of words with a frequency below one per million tokens on the uniform frequency resource, mean rated age of acquisition, mean orthographic length, mean per-token surprisal under a language-specific neural language model, lexical density, the Measure of Textual Lexical Diversity and concreteness. *Grammatical* features are mean dependency distance from a universal-dependencies parse, clauses per sentence, the ratio of subordinate to main clauses, mean sentence length and mean depth of noun-phrase modification. *Discourse* features are mean semantic similarity between adjacent sentences from a multilingual sentence encoder, the proportion of adjacent sentence pairs sharing a referring expression, connectives per hundred words by relation type and narrativity. *Affective* features are the mean and the variability of valence and of arousal.

Supplementary Table 3 gives the primary and the sensitivity resource for each feature family, with its coverage across the ten languages the structural sample showed. The ten languages are Dutch, English, French, German, Greek, Italian, Korean, Polish, Portuguese and Spanish. Four rules govern that table and are fixed before any feature is computed. The first addresses a problem specific to multilingual work: a variable measured by a different instrument in each language confounds the method of measurement with the language, so that a language-level slope no longer means the same thing twice over. Each feature will therefore be computed from a single resource applied identically in every language, even where a better native resource exists in one of them, and native norms will be run as a pre-specified sensitivity analysis with the per-language correlation between the two reported. Second, no value is ever carried across languages by translating a word list, and a predicted resource is admitted only where the prediction was made within each language by one documented procedure and its correlation with native ratings is reported. Where no acceptable measure exists for a language, that language does not contribute that feature. Third, every measure reports the proportion of tokens it matched, and a language in which a measure matches fewer than 80 per cent of tokens does not contribute it. A per-text rule under the dimension reduction governs which texts enter the component solution. Fourth, the full inventory, the software versions, the model checkpoints, the tokenisation rules and the matched-token proportions will be frozen and published before any feature is joined to an outcome. Korean is the language these rules constrain most, and the consequences for it are set out beside that table.

### Measures

The processing outcome, serving Hypotheses 1 to 4 and 6, is the natural logarithm of elapsed reading time divided by the story's word count, standardised within reading language. We describe it throughout as reading pace or processing time, never as a measure of comprehension or fluency, because nothing in these data licenses that reading. The outcome for Hypothesis 5 is the child's optional post-reading rating of the story as easy, just right or difficult, treated as ordered and modelled on a cumulative-logit scale.

The confirmatory predictors are the three component scores defined below. Text length in words, narrativity, mean valence and mean arousal are pre-specified secondary text predictors and enter every model as covariates. The variability of valence and of arousal, and the additive and temporal connective densities, will be computed for description only: they enter no confirmatory model and are excluded from the component solution. Whether the text was generated or drawn from the classic set enters as a covariate, and the substantive comparison between the two is a contingent hypothesis, for reasons given under @tbl-unresolved. Because predictors are standardised within language, a pooled coefficient is an average over languages of slopes each expressed in that language's own standard-deviation units. We will report the raw-scale standard deviation of each component per language so that readers can translate, and the language-varying slopes summarise the heterogeneity this induces.

Three variables describe the reader and the reading context. The age band is the platform's own record of the child's age group, reduced to the two bands this study covers. The band is taken per session. An account whose recorded band changes within the window contributes each session under the band recorded for it, and the number of such accounts will be reported. The reading level is the level the family has set for the session, which determines which version of a text is served and is therefore an attribute of the reading as well as of the reader. Narration is the session-level flag recording that a spoken rendition accompanied the reading. All three are chosen by the family and none is randomised.

Accumulated in-app reading, which serves Hypothesis 6, is the cumulative count of words in completed distinct stories the account read before the current session, on a log scale. Session order, the number of days since the account's previous eligible session and the number of days since the account's first eligible session enter alongside it, so that accumulated reading is separated from the position of a session in a sequence, from recency and from the time elapsed since entry. Within tier 2 the measure is decomposed into the account's own mean and the current session's deviation from it, and the deviation term is the registered test.

The data are crossed, and not nested: readings sit within accounts, a text is met by many accounts and exists in several languages and at several reading levels, and an account may read in more than one language. We will therefore treat Account, Text, Language, Country and App version as crossed grouping factors, and report the counts supporting each before fitting any model. A grouping factor other than Text and Account enters when it has at least five levels with at least 20 eligible readings each. Below that it is dropped, and the drop will be reported. Reading level, with only three levels, enters as a fixed factor. If at least 90 per cent of texts are read in only one eligible session, a Text varying intercept is not estimable and is replaced by varying intercepts for the repeated attribute combination that generated the text. These thresholds are registered conventions, and any consequence of them will be reported.

### Randomisation and blinding

Nothing in this study is randomised. It is a secondary analysis of records generated by families using a commercial application, and no allocation, assignment or condition is under anyone's control. The only random assignment anywhere in the protocol is the permutation quality check, where we reassign texts to readings at random precisely to destroy the association under test.

Data collection and analysis will not be performed blind to the conditions of the study. Data collection is performed by the platform without researcher involvement. Before in-principle acceptance, blinding is structural: we cannot see the outcome data because the data controller holds them, under the sequestration arrangement described above. After transfer, analysis will not be blind to the values of the predictors or grouping variables, since the registered models require them. We will write, run and debug the outcome-model code against data simulated from the design specification deposited with this protocol, so that every script is complete and exercised before the real file exists on any machine of ours.

## Sampling plan

The design is observational and the sample is a census: we will analyse every eligible record in one immutable extract, whose closing date is fixed before any outcome model is fitted, with no sequential testing and no optional stopping.

Two nested samples serve different hypotheses, because those hypotheses are identified at different levels and the data supporting them are unequally certain.

Tier 1 carries the text hypotheses. It comprises every completed reading in the extract for which the account is recorded in age band 7-8 or 9 and over, the reading language is one the text-feature pipeline covers, the story text has been supplied, and the reading time falls inside the plausibility bounds below. Where an account read the same text more than once, only the first reading enters tier 1, and repeated readings are retained for the practice analysis described under sensitivity. The unit of analysis is one reading of one text by one account.

Whether tier 1 can estimate a child varying intercept depends on how many accounts read more than one distinct text, which is not known in advance. If at least ten per cent of tier-1 readings come from accounts contributing two or more readings, the model includes a varying intercept for Account. If fewer do, that term is not separable from residual variance: it is dropped, child variance is carried in the residual, and the reduction in the effective independence of the sample is stated wherever a tier-1 interval is reported. The ten per cent figure is a registered convention. We will read the proportion from the provider-computed counts before fitting anything.

Tier 2 carries the within-child hypothesis. It comprises those tier-1 accounts contributing at least three eligible readings of distinct texts. Three is the smallest number that leaves a degree of freedom once a within-child slope and an intercept are estimated, and the threshold will be varied to two and to five in the sensitivity analyses. Tier 2 estimates a child varying intercept and separates each child's mean level of a predictor from that reading's deviation from it, so a within-child association is not conflated with stable differences between children who habitually read at different rates. How many accounts reach the tier-2 threshold is not known in advance. The structural sample contains none, but it holds one session per account and cannot speak to the full window.

Reading time enters as elapsed seconds for the whole story divided by the story's word count, and we bound it by what a child could physically be doing, and not by anything observed in these data. We will exclude a reading faster than 400 words per minute, or 0.15 seconds per word, as faster than reading. We will exclude a reading slower than 10 words per minute, or six seconds per word, as a story left open. The upper bound follows a published precedent that states such a rule and its yield: a meta-analysis of Spanish reading rates deleted silent rates above 400 words per minute, on the ground that such a rate exceeds what a competent adult can manage and indicates skipped text [@raynerSoMuchRead2016], removing 313 of 19,237 cases [@ripollsalcedaReadingRateSpanish2020]. The lower bound sits below the slowest pooled mean in that meta-analysis, 30 words per minute for Spanish first-graders reading silently, though not below the floor of the normal range proposed for that grade, 8 words per minute. From second grade the range begins at 41. A floor of 10 words per minute can therefore exclude a genuinely slow reader only among the youngest first-graders, most of whom the age criterion removes in any case. Both bounds are wide by design, so the primary analysis removes little beyond the impossible. Tighter treatments are sensitivity analyses. We will report the number and proportion removed by every rule, by language, age band, reading level and narration state.

One further rule concerns the top of the distribution. Where a session timeout caps the recorded interval, the cap shows itself as an implausible number of sessions sharing one value, which is one of the quantities the provider-computed counts report. If those counts show more than one per cent of sessions sharing a single value, we will locate that value in the transferred extract before fitting any outcome model. If it lies in the upper decile of the reading-time distribution, we will treat it as a right-censoring point and fit the timing models as censored lognormal models, with those observations censored, and not discarded.

Ahead of all of the above, we will exclude sessions the platform flags as incomplete or crashed, duplicated event records, accounts flagged as duplicates under the platform's own data-quality rules, and stories without a positive word count. No excluded datum is replaced. A participant-flow diagram will report every exclusion and the retained accounts, readings and texts, overall and by language.

### Measurement, availability and missingness audit

Measurement error in digital traces has its own taxonomy, and the errors specific to platform data are not the errors of surveys [@senTotalErrorFramework2021]. Of the error types that framework names, four apply here. The platform defines the categories, so age band and reading level are its constructs. The instrument drifts, because the app changes version across the window. The interval that the timing column covers is not fully specified, which is question (c). And a session timeout would right-censor the outcome, which is why the censoring rule is registered in advance. None of these is fatal, and each is one of the reasons the audit precedes the models.

Before fitting any outcome model, we will run and archive an audit of the frozen extract and its dictionary. It establishes field availability and units, the granularity of the age field, how often a text and a reading level recur, the narration flag's behaviour within accounts and within sessions, duplicate and crash flags, changes across app versions, per-language feature coverage, and every nesting and crossing count the models require. It also reports missingness for every planned variable, overall and by language, age band, reading level, narration state and session order.

Three rules govern what the audit may change. A feature that is structurally unavailable in a language is not imputed: the language simply does not contribute it. A session missing an outcome is excluded from the model for that outcome alone, and a missing narration flag does not remove a session from a model that has no narration term. No variable is selected, transformed or discarded because of its association with reading time or with the rating.

The rating in Hypothesis 5 is optional and was absent for 25 of the 35 sessions in the structural sample, so high missingness is expected. Where the rating is missing for more than five per cent of otherwise eligible sessions, we will model availability from observed pre-response variables and report an inverse-probability-weighted analysis as a sensitivity check, with weight distributions and common support shown.

### Design and precision analysis

Nature Human Behaviour's guidelines set 0.95 as the a priori power floor for frequentist plans and, for Bayesian plans, allow a maximum feasible sample provided an inconclusive result at that size would still be an important message. This design is neither a significance test nor a Bayes-factor test but an estimation design on a census of existing records, and it maps onto the second provision. The frozen extract is the maximum feasible sample, since no further data can be collected, and 0.90 is registered as the assurance level at which a hypothesis counts as adequately powered, with every 0.95 requirement reported beside it from the same archived curves (Supplementary Section S5) so that a reader can apply the stricter target. An inconclusive verdict at the census is itself informative. If the extract holds too few distinct texts, we will say so before fitting and report that this platform cannot answer the question, which matters for a class of data source that others will be tempted to use. A hypothesis declared underpowered is still fitted and reported, so its interval bounds the effect even where it cannot decide it.

Because we will analyse every eligible record, the question is not how large a sample to collect but what the available records can settle. Here that turns on a single quantity: the text coefficients are identified between distinct texts, and how many distinct texts the extract holds is unresolved.

We therefore simulated data from the design specifications deposited alongside this protocol with pilotr, sweeping the number of distinct texts at constant readings per text and separately sweeping readings per text at a constant number of texts [@bernabeuPilotr2026]. The simulated tier-1 model contained the three components, the age band, the two age-band interactions and a text intercept, fitted by maximum likelihood. The narration model contained the lexical and continuity components, the narration flag and their interactions with it. The tier-2 model added a child intercept and a single accumulated-reading trend. The simulated models therefore omit the narration terms of the tier-1 model, the reading-level adjustment, the covariates, the language, country and app-version intercepts, the language-varying slopes, the distributional sub-model and the review-derived priors that the registered models carry. Simulation was on the within-language standardised scale, with the text intercept contributing 9 per cent of the variance, the child intercept 20 per cent and the residual the remainder, so a simulated coefficient is directly comparable with the region of practical equivalence. The simulation generated child variance and then handed the analysis a dataset in which each account contributes one reading, so that variance reached the fitted model as inflated residual, and in that one respect the requirements below are an upper bound on what the design needs. The omissions do not all point the same way. Adjusting for reading level, which moves all three feature families together, will remove some of the components' variance and raise every requirement, whereas the language-varying slopes and the priors will lower them. The simulation balanced the age band and narration, and the main effects it priced are balanced averages. The registered prevalence-weighted main effects carry the precision of the pooled slope and no design effect, whereas each interaction inherits the design effect for imbalance that the adjustments below apply. We will refit one grid point of each sweep with the registered brms specification when the design analysis is re-run at the observed inputs, and report the difference. A coefficient the size of the region can never be declared determinately outside it, so we ran the sweep at twice that size, the smallest effect this protocol treats as worth reporting. A null condition with every coefficient set to zero established how reliably the design can declare practical equivalence, so an inconclusive verdict is predictable in advance.

The region of 0.05 standard deviations and the 0.10-standard-deviation effect are registered conventions, the second being twice the first because an effect at the boundary can never be declared outside it. The accompanying review supplies the check on them. The prior-derivation pipeline (Supplementary Section S6) will record, before any outcome datum is accessed, whether each component's pooled estimate on the model's scale exceeds 0.10 standard deviations. Where a pooled estimate lies between 0.05 and 0.10, the texts sweep will be re-simulated with the deposited scripts at that effect, replacing the single 0.10 input, and the resulting threshold replaces the one in @tbl-design for that component before fitting. Where a pooled estimate lies at or below the region's half-width, no number of texts could yield a determinate verdict at that size. The 0.10 convention then stands, and the discrepancy will be reported beside the component's verdict.

For the three text coefficients, an effect of 0.10 standard deviations reached a determinate verdict nine times in ten at 738 distinct texts for lexical difficulty (95 per cent interval 640 to 843), 660 for grammatical load (593 to 731) and 634 for referential continuity (568 to 704), and 95 times in 100 at 926, 812 and 784. The interactions with the age band needed roughly twice as many: 1,230 texts for grammatical load (1,107 to 1,359) and 1,431 for referential continuity (1,276 to 1,596) at 0.90, and 1,510 for grammatical load at 0.95, a target the continuity interaction did not reach within the 1,600 texts simulated. The narration contrast needed 1,234 texts (1,113 to 1,361) before the design effect for imbalance is applied, and 1,506 at 0.95. That figure prices the lexical-by-narration interaction coefficient, and is a lower bound for the difference-of-proportions rule Hypothesis 4 registers, whose draw-by-draw ratio has heavier tails than the coefficient it is built from. Declaring practical equivalence when there is nothing there cost about the same: at 800 texts a main effect was correctly declared equivalent in 87 to 90 per cent of replicates and at 1,600 in every one, while the interactions reached 89 to 92 per cent only at 1,600, over 120 replicates. An inconclusive verdict is therefore predictable from the number of texts alone. The within-child term needed 563 children in tier 2 (463 to 674) contributing five readings each, and 681 (543 to 834) at 0.95, for the unadjusted trend. The registered term is adjusted for session order and elapsed time, with which accumulated words are correlated within a child, so this figure understates the requirement, and the tier-2 re-run described below re-derives it with those covariates in place.

The second sweep is the more instructive. Holding the number of distinct texts at 250 and raising readings per text from 2 to 60 narrowed the interval on a main effect from 0.19 to 0.08 standard deviations, yet never carried it to a determinate verdict, reaching 0.70 at best. Over the same range the age-band interactions climbed from under 0.11 to between 0.87 and 0.90. Sessions and texts are therefore not interchangeable: a text coefficient is bounded by how many different texts the platform generated, whereas an interaction between a text property and a reader attribute gains from many different children meeting the same text. This matters because sessions are the quantity this platform has in abundance and distinct texts are the quantity in doubt, so a very large export could still leave Hypothesis 1 underpowered while answering Hypotheses 2 and 3.

@fig-precision shows both sweeps. The threshold each hypothesis has to clear is recorded in @tbl-design, and we fixed it before the extract was released. A hypothesis whose required contrast is absent will be labelled untestable, and one whose simulated interval cannot separate the region's boundary from the effect will be declared underpowered, before its model is fitted.

Five adjustments of the design analysis are registered, each a function of the provider-computed counts or of the archived prior pipeline. Two are analytic. The simulation balances the narration contrast, whereas narration was on in 32 of the 35 sessions of the structural sample. An unbalanced binary contrast at prevalence $p$ inflates the variance of its interaction coefficient by $1/(4p(1-p))$ relative to balance, so we will multiply the simulated Hypothesis 4 requirement by that factor at the observed narration prevalence and state the adjusted requirement before fitting. At a narration prevalence of 0.91, equivalently an unnarrated share of 0.09, the factor is about 3.0. The second adjustment applies the same factor to the Hypothesis 2 and 3 requirements at the observed age-band prevalence, since the simulation balanced the bands as well. Two are re-runs of the deposited scripts. The rating simulation will be re-run at the observed rating availability, replacing that single input. The tier-2 sweep will be re-run at the observed distribution of sessions per child, and for that re-run alone the deposited tier-2 specification will be extended with session order and days since the first session, with per-session word counts generated so that accumulated words correlate with session order as the counts show. The extended specification will be deposited before it is run. The thresholds those re-runs yield replace the ones in @tbl-design for the underpowered declarations of Hypotheses 5 and 6. The fifth adjustment is the re-simulation at a pooled effect below 0.10 described above, which runs only if the prior pipeline calls for it.

## Analysis plan

We will fit all confirmatory models as Bayesian hierarchical models with the brms package and its Stan backend [@burknerBrmsPackageBayesian2017], standardising continuous predictors within language after transformation. Wherever the accompanying systematic review supports it, weakly informative priors will be replaced by priors derived from that review, as described under Priors.

### Outcome-blind dimension reduction

As recorded under Data provenance, none of what follows has been run, and the first fitting will follow in-principle acceptance. The observed text features are correlated because the same decision about what reading level a text is written for moves lexical, grammatical and discourse properties together. We will use principal component analysis to reduce them without treating them as effects of an unobserved latent cause [@crossleyDevelopingLinguisticConstructs2025], and will conduct it separately within the lexical, grammatical and discourse families. The affective measures will be kept as separate secondary predictors, because valence and arousal are theoretically distinct and need not move together. Narrativity, though computed as a discourse feature, will likewise be excluded from the component solution, because it enters every model as a separate secondary predictor and must not sit on both sides. Each distinct text will contribute one row regardless of how often it was read, so a popular text does not determine the solution, and a text enters a family's solution only if it has valid values on every retained feature of that family.

Counts will be transformed with $\log(1+x)$ and bounded proportions with an empirical-logit transform where these reduce skew. A feature is dropped from a language if more than 20 per cent of values are missing, if fewer than 80 per cent of texts receive a valid token-level match, or if its standard deviation after transformation is below 0.01. A language contributes to a family's solution only if it has at least 100 distinct eligible texts and at least three valid features in that family, two of them anchors. Where two features correlate at $|r| > .90$, the retained one is chosen in this order: lower missingness, then broader language coverage, then higher extraction reliability on a manually checked sample, then the measure listed first under Materials. No outcome correlation enters any of these decisions.

Features will be standardised within language. To stop the largest language determining the solution, we will compute a correlation matrix within each eligible language, transform the correlations to Fisher's *z*, average the matrices with equal weight per language, and transform the average back before the analysis [@revelleRPackagePsych2023]. Sampling adequacy requires individual Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin values above .50 and an overall value above .60. The number of components will be set by parallel analysis against the 95th percentile of 10,000 random datasets [@hornRationaleTestNumber1965]. The scree plot will be reported but does not override that rule. Where a family retains more than one component, we will use promax rotation with $\kappa$ = 4, because linguistic properties may correlate [@biberVariationSpeechWriting1988]. We will then apply the regression scoring coefficients from the frozen, language-balanced solution to each text's within-language standardised features.

Each confirmatory component must load at least .30 in absolute value on at least two of its anchors. For LexicalDifficulty, the anchors are frequency, surprisal and word length. For GrammaticalLoad, they are dependency distance, subordination, clause density, sentence length and noun-phrase depth. For ReferentialContinuity, they are adjacent-sentence similarity, referential overlap and the density of causal and contrastive connectives. Age of acquisition contributes to the lexical family where a broad native norm set exists but is not an anchor, because the cross-linguistic set holds only 299 words per language. Only the causal and contrastive connective densities enter the discourse family, and both are anchors. The additive and temporal densities are descriptive only, as stated under Measures. The restriction is substantive: in 794 readers across 20 texts, causal and contrastive connectives raised comprehension, temporal ones did nothing and additive ones lowered it, so a single mixed count has no defined expected sign [@kleijnComprehensionEffectsConnectives2019]. Signs are fixed so that higher LexicalDifficulty and GrammaticalLoad mean a more demanding text and higher ReferentialContinuity a more explicitly connected one. If no component in a family satisfies the rule, the hypotheses resting on that family are reported as untestable. The complete pattern matrix, the component correlations, the variance explained, the language-specific matrices and the loading congruence for the five largest languages will be reported. Language-specific and sparse solutions are sensitivity analyses, and never alternative routes chosen after seeing an outcome.

### Confirmatory models

In tier 1, we will estimate a model of within-language standardised log reading time per word with the three components, the age band, the narration flag, the interactions of each component with the age band and with narration, the reading level, log text length, narrativity, valence, arousal and the generated-or-classic indicator as fixed effects, with the age band and narration entered as deviations from their observed prevalence as stated in the Introduction. Its grouping structure comprises varying intercepts for Text, Country and App version, varying intercepts and uncorrelated component slopes for Language, and a varying intercept for Account where the estimability rule above is met. Hypotheses 1 to 4 will be evaluated in this model. The slope of a component in a given state is recovered draw by draw as the main effect plus the interaction multiplied by that state's deviation score, so that the unnarrated slope is the main effect plus the narration interaction times the unnarrated deviation score, which is zero minus the narration prevalence, and the narrated slope is the main effect plus the interaction times one minus the prevalence.

The Hypothesis 4 contrast will be computed as follows. For each posterior draw, the proportional attenuation of a component is one minus its narrated slope divided by its unnarrated slope, so that a positive value means a smaller coefficient under narration. The gate registered in the Introduction is evaluated on the derived unnarrated slopes: the contrast is computed only when fewer than 5 per cent of the draws of each unnarrated slope lie inside the region of practical equivalence. Draws in which either unnarrated slope lies inside the region will be excluded from the ratio, and the excluded fraction will be reported. As a registered sensitivity analysis, the contrast will be repeated with a fixed denominator, each narration interaction divided by the posterior median of its unnarrated slope, and reported beside the draw-by-draw version.

Three further rules govern Hypothesis 4. First, the within-account contrast, restricted to accounts observed in both narration states, becomes the primary Hypothesis 4 estimate if those accounts cover at least as many distinct texts as the adjusted requirement, with the full-sample contrast reported beside it. Otherwise the within-account contrast remains a sensitivity analysis, and the selection into narration state is named wherever the full-sample estimate is reported. Second, the tier-1 model carries a distributional sub-model in which the residual standard deviation is itself predicted by the narration flag, and the ratio of the narrated to the unnarrated residual standard deviation is the compression diagnostic. A ratio below 0.5 is the registered signature of a recording setting the pace. If it fires, the full-sample contrast is not interpreted and Hypothesis 4 rests on the subset described next. Third, the contrast will be repeated in the narrated sessions the audio cannot have paced. For each language, the narration rate will be estimated as the median words per minute of its narrated sessions, and a narrated session counts as unpaced when its rate exceeds 1.5 times that median. Where a language has fewer than 100 narrated sessions, a fixed bound applies instead: that language's own adult read-aloud mean in the International Reading Speed Texts where the language is among the 17 covered, and otherwise the slowest of those means, 138 words per minute for Arabic [@trauzettelklosinskiStandardizedAssessmentReading2012]. The premise, stated here so that the audio duration would let it be checked, is that a narration recorded for children is paced no faster than adult oral reading in the same language. If the selectivity survives where the recording was not the constraint, pacing does not explain it. Hypothesis 4 is reported as underpowered from the subset if the subset holds fewer distinct texts than the adjusted requirement. Should the data controller supply the audio duration, these rules are replaced by the duration itself and we will report the substitution as a deviation from this protocol.

The Hypothesis 5 model will have the same fixed and grouping structure and a cumulative-logit likelihood over the three rating categories, with category thresholds allowed to vary by language so that a difference in how families in different countries use the middle category is not read as a difference in text difficulty. A text rated by fewer than five distinct children does not contribute, and the primary model is complete-case, with the inverse-probability sensitivity analysis registered under the audit.

For tier 2, we will refit the same specification with a varying intercept for Account, decomposing accumulated reading into the account's mean and the current session's deviation from it, alongside session order, days since the previous session and days since the account's first eligible session. The deviation term is the registered test for Hypothesis 6.

Posterior predictive checks will assess calibration and residual structure by language, age band, reading level and narration state in every model.

### Priors

For each confirmatory main effect, and for the secondary text predictors where the review holds at least two studies for them, priors will be derived from the accompanying systematic review through a deterministic pipeline whose rules we froze before any extraction row existed, and which will be run, with its output archived, before any outcome datum is accessed. The review's extracted estimates for the corresponding predictor family and outcome class will be sign-harmonised so that facilitation always means faster reading, converted to a common standardised scale, and pooled by random-effects meta-analysis with one estimate per study per relation. The prior is Student's $t(3, \hat\mu, \sigma)$, where $\hat\mu$ is the pooled estimate translated to the model's scale and $\sigma$ is twice the combined pooling and between-study uncertainty, with a floor of 0.10. The doubling and the floor guard against the gap between a laboratory comprehension test and a passively timed reading in a game.

The same review motivates the hypotheses, so the evidence that generates a prediction also centres its prior, and a reviewer is entitled to ask whether that makes a predicted verdict easier to reach. Inference here is estimation against a region, and not a Bayes factor, so a prior centred in the predicted direction does not enter the decision as a hypothesis weight. The doubled scale and heavy tails make the derived priors weakly informative relative to the likelihood that hundreds of texts will supply. And we will report prior-data conflict diagnostics for every review-derived prior. We register the tie-break as well: the fit with the derived priors carries the registered verdict, and a hypothesis whose label changes under the weakly informative refit described next is reported as sensitive to the prior and is not counted as a determinate confirmatory verdict.

Coefficients without adequate review evidence, which means every interaction term and any family supported by fewer than two studies, keep weakly informative priors: $t(3, 0, 0.5)$ for standardised main effects and $t(3, 0, 0.25)$ for interactions. Group-level and residual standard deviations take half-$t(3, 0, 1)$ priors and any estimated correlation matrix takes LKJ($\eta$ = 2). Intercept priors will be calibrated by prior-predictive simulation to the outcome scale, without reference to any predictor-outcome association. The derivation rules are summarised in Supplementary Section S6, and the full prior table with its forest plots will be archived before the extract is transferred and will accompany the Stage 2 report. We will refit every model with weakly informative priors throughout, and with the derived scales halved and doubled, and report conclusions under each.

### Decision rules and diagnostics

For every confirmatory coefficient, we will report the posterior median, the 95 per cent highest-density interval, the probability of the predicted direction, the proportion of the posterior inside the region of practical equivalence, and a model-implied contrast on an interpretable scale. The region is $|\beta| < 0.05$ standard deviations for a one-standard-deviation change in a predictor of reading time, and a half-width of log(1.05) on the log-odds scale for the rating model. More than 95 per cent of the posterior inside the region is read as practical equivalence, and less than 5 per cent inside it as a practically non-negligible association, labelled as in the predicted direction or in the opposite direction according to the sign of the posterior median. Everything else is inconclusive. For the ordering clause of Hypothesis 5, a posterior probability of at least 0.90 that the three coefficients rank as they do for reading time counts as agreement on order, and anything lower as order not established. For Hypothesis 4, at least 95 per cent of the posterior of the difference of attenuations above 0.20 supports selective removal of decoding cost, more than 95 per cent inside the region supports audio pacing, more than 95 per cent below -0.05 is reverse selectivity, and anything else is inconclusive. The fixed-denominator sensitivity contrast is read against the same thresholds.

Each hypothesis is a single pre-registered test with its own decision rule, and no claim in this protocol aggregates evidence across hypotheses, so no correction for multiple comparisons will be applied. The one composite claim, the overall Hypothesis 1 verdict, is an intersection-union rule: it is recorded only when all three coefficients are individually non-negligible in the predicted direction, so its error rate cannot exceed that of any single component. Hierarchical shrinkage and the null condition of the design analysis, which reports how often a zero effect is wrongly declared non-negligible, calibrate the per-decision error rates behind @tbl-design.

Four registered contingencies read fitted quantities after fitting, and none of them changes whether a hypothesis is tested, on which sample, or with which model. The first is the Hypothesis 4 compression diagnostic, which withholds the full-sample contrast. The second is the exclusion of draws with an unnarrated slope inside the region from the Hypothesis 4 ratio. The third is the third outcome-neutral check, which makes the within-level estimate primary for a component whose pooled coefficient it halves. The fourth is the prior-sensitivity label above. Each is stated where it applies, and each is an IF-THEN rule fixed here.

We will run four chains of 4,000 iterations, half of them warm-up. Acceptable sampling requires $\hat{R}$ below 1.01, bulk and tail effective sample sizes above 1,000 for every confirmatory parameter, no divergent transitions, satisfactory energy diagnostics and no unresolved maximum-treedepth warnings. Models failing these will be refitted with a higher target acceptance rate, greater tree depth and more iterations. If simplification is still needed, language-level slopes will be removed in the fixed order lexical, then discourse, then grammatical, and every estimable varying intercept will be retained. Every simplification and its diagnostic consequence will be reported. Variance inflation factors will be reported for the fixed-effect design matrix. A high value does not trigger an outcome-dependent deletion: the joint model remains primary, and single-family models will be reported as a collinearity sensitivity analysis.

For Hypotheses 2, 3 and 4, we will compare the model with one omitting the relevant interaction, using Pareto-smoothed importance-sampling leave-one-out cross-validation, and report the expected log pointwise predictive density difference, its standard error and the Pareto-$k$ diagnostics, with exact refits where importance sampling is unreliable. Predictive comparison supplements the coefficient-level summaries and does not gate them.

### Outcome-neutral quality checks

Five checks will run before the confirmatory models are interpreted, each with a stated pass criterion and a stated consequence of failure, and a sixth, the ordering clause of Hypothesis 5, is evaluated with that hypothesis. The first, second, fourth and sixth are decided without reference to any confirmatory coefficient. The third is a robustness condition computed from the fitted text coefficients, and the fifth is a registered clause of Hypothesis 5.

The first is a permutation null. We will reassign texts at random to readings within language and reading level, and refit the tier-1 model 200 times. The refits will use the maximum-likelihood analogue of the tier-1 model, with the same fixed and estimable grouping structure, and the region will be applied to the 95 per cent Wald interval, since 200 full Bayesian refits are not feasible and the check concerns leakage rather than calibration. No text coefficient may be declared practically non-negligible in more than 5 per cent of those refits. An inconclusive verdict on permuted data is the expected outcome at moderate text counts and does not count as failure. A coefficient that survives permutation means the pipeline is carrying structure that does not come from the pairing of a text with a reading, and we will withhold the confirmatory results until the leak is found and reported.

The second is a positive control on the timing column. Total elapsed time must rise with the story's word count, with more than 99 per cent of the posterior above zero. This is close to a tautology if the column means what the dictionary says it means, which is why its failure would be informative: a timing field dominated by idle or backgrounded time need not track how much text there was to read. Failure means the timing column does not index reading, and Hypotheses 1 to 4 and 6 are reported as not evaluable on this extract.

The third asks whether the association is an artefact of platform assignment. We will re-estimate the three text coefficients within each reading level separately, and each must retain at least half the magnitude it had in the pooled model. The account on which text difficulty is merely assigned to children who differ in capacity predicts that these coefficients shrink towards zero when the level is held fixed. The account this protocol advances predicts that they do not. This check is a robustness condition and not a decision about testing: if a coefficient falls below half its pooled magnitude, the within-level estimate becomes the primary estimate for that component and the pooled one is reported beside it, with the assignment confound named wherever the coefficient appears.

The fourth is a set of three independence claims the theory object entails. Conditional on the reading level and on whether a text was generated or classic, the three components should be close to independent across texts. Narration should be unrelated to accumulated reading. And the difficulty rating should carry no further information about reading level once reading time is conditioned on. We will report each as an estimate with an interval, and an implication is judged to have failed when the 95 per cent interval of the corresponding conditional association lies entirely beyond 0.10 in standardised units. A failure does not invalidate the confirmatory tests, but it identifies a path the causal diagram omits, and it is reported as such.

The fifth is convergent validity, the ordering clause of Hypothesis 5, specified there and evaluated with it, with its outcome under an underpowered Hypothesis 5 stated there.

The sixth is a validation of the feature pipeline itself. We will check a stratified random sample of 50 texts per language by hand for tokenisation, sentence splitting and dependency attachment, and report the agreement statistics per language before any feature is joined to an outcome. A language whose labelled-attachment agreement with the hand-checked parse falls below .85 contributes to descriptive reporting but not to the grammatical component.

### Sensitivity analyses

The following sensitivity analyses are pre-specified. We will refit the timing models with no plausibility bounds at all, with winsorisation at the 1st and 99th and at the 0.5th and 99.5th percentiles within language, and with posterior-predictive residual trimming. Where the censoring rule is triggered, we will report the censored and uncensored fits side by side. We will vary the tier-2 threshold from three distinct texts to two and to five, and add repeated readings with a repetition indicator. We will restrict analyses to the five largest languages, and fit language-specific models and component solutions with loading congruence reported. We will replace the component scores with sparse-component scores and with pre-specified equal-weight composites of the anchor features. Where the audit finds the age field finer than two bands, we will re-estimate the Hypothesis 2 and 3 interactions with age entered as an ordinal monotonic predictor and report the result beside the two-band contrast. For narration, we will report the within-account contrast where it is not already primary, and the fixed-denominator contrast registered under Confirmatory models. We will compare the rating model under adjacent-category and cumulative-logit links, stratify it by language, and compare the inverse-probability analysis for rating non-response with the complete-case estimates. We will compare Text grouping with grouping on the attribute combination that generated the text. Finally, we will halve and double the prior scales and apply the alternative regions of practical equivalence, 0.03 and 0.10 standard deviations for reading time and half-widths of log(1.03) and log(1.10) on the log-odds scale for the rating.

To ease comparison with the prior literature, we will report maximum-likelihood mixed models with the same fixed and estimable grouping structure in a supplementary table. They are descriptive, carry no confirmatory weight, and will not be used to resolve a Bayesian result.

### What is not yet settled, and what follows from each answer

We put thirteen questions about the extract to the data controller on 7 August 2026, and they remain open at submission. Leaving them open is not a gap in the protocol so long as each has a decision rule attached in advance, and @tbl-unresolved attaches one to each. Every rule below is a function of the answer alone.

Five of these questions correspond to auxiliary assumptions recorded in the theory object, which is how the protocol keeps the statistical contingency and the theoretical commitment in the same place. If the answer to a question falsifies its assumption, the predictions that assumption protects are the ones the table reassigns.

### Contingent hypotheses

We specify four further hypotheses in full here, outside the confirmatory set, because each depends on a fact about the extract that the data controller has not yet confirmed. Each carries an activation rule, and the rule is a function of that fact alone, read from the controller's written answer or, for the requirement that accounts be observed in both narration states, from the provider-computed counts.

A contingent hypothesis activates only if its condition is confirmed in writing by the data controller before this protocol is submitted, and the confirmation is reproduced in Supplementary Section S7. A condition confirmed after submission does not activate anything: the hypothesis is then reported at Stage 2 as exploratory, under that label, and is not counted among the confirmatory tests. This asymmetry is deliberate, because a hypothesis activated after review has not been reviewed. At submission, no condition has been confirmed, so none of the four is activated, and Supplementary Section S7 records that. They are retained here so that, should a condition be confirmed later, the analysis reported at Stage 2 under Exploratory analyses is the one written before any data were seen. A hypothesis whose condition is never confirmed is not run.

*C1: coherence and inferential comprehension.* Condition: item-level comprehension responses exist and carry a recoverable question type. We would predict that, in an item-level model of response correctness, ReferentialContinuity × QuestionType is positive with inference questions coded 1 and literal questions 0, so that the association of continuity with correctness is larger where the question requires integration [@freedAssessmentInferencemakingChildren2021; @pickrenContributionTextCharacteristics2022; @aparicioComprehensionPerformancesExplanatory2022].

*C2: narration and comprehension.* Condition: item-level comprehension responses exist, and accounts are observed both with and without narration. We would predict that, within an account, narration is positively associated with response correctness after text, age band, reading level, accumulated reading and language are adjusted for. The expected size is small [@clintonlisellDoesReadingWhile2023; @woodUseTexttoSpeech2018], and the coefficient identifies an association, and never an effect.

*C3: reading pace and comprehension.* Condition: as C2, restricted to sessions without narration. We would predict that an account's mean log reading time per word is negatively associated with response correctness, so that accounts with a faster habitual pace answer more accurately [@sortkaerBothSidesStory2021]. The simultaneous within-account deviation term keeps this between-account association distinct from a difficult or interrupted session.

*C4: machine-generated against human-authored text.* Condition: the classic stories are confirmed to be fixed, human-authored texts, identical for all users within a language. We would predict that the three text components predict reading pace with coefficients of the same sign in generated and in classic texts, and that the interaction of each component with the generated-or-classic indicator is practically equivalent to zero under the registered region. This is a test of exchangeability, and not of quality, and the closest existing evidence is the adult eye-movement corpus on machine-generated text [@bolligerEMTeCCorpusEye2025]. A non-negligible interaction would mean that the properties governing how children read human-written stories govern their reading of generated ones differently.

## Timeline

The export is built and held before submission, so the study can begin on the day in-principle acceptance is confirmed. We anticipate transfer of the extract within four weeks of that confirmation; the frozen audit, the feature extraction with its hand-checked validation, and the outcome-blind dimension reduction within three months of transfer; the confirmatory and sensitivity models within a further four months; and submission of the Stage 2 manuscript within twelve months of in-principle acceptance. [The author to confirm or adjust these intervals.] Any extension would be negotiated with the handling editor.

# Data availability

The session-level extract is held by the data controller and is not in our possession at submission. On in-principle acceptance it will be transferred under a data-sharing agreement between the University of Oxford and the data controller. On acceptance of the Stage 2 manuscript we will deposit, in [the named public repository, with a digital object identifier], the story texts, the computed text features, the component scores, the fitted model objects, the participant-flow counts, the laboratory log, and every table and figure underlying the reported results. Session-level fields that the agreement classes as commercially sensitive may be restricted. For each such field we will state the reason and deposit a derived form sufficient to reproduce every reported analysis, and interested researchers will be able to request the restricted fields through [the named data controller contact or the mechanism the agreement specifies]. The file manifest and the provider-computed aggregate counts contain no record of any individual and will be deposited in the same repository on receipt, before in-principle acceptance. The 35-row structural sample described under Pilot data is deposited there for peer review, under embargo until Stage 2 acceptance, with a view-only link supplied to the editors.

# Code availability

All analysis code is version-controlled at <https://github.com/pablobernabeu/InTRACt_Interplay_of_Text_Reader_And_Context>, in the `preregistration` directory, which will be public and complete at submission and is available for peer review. The theory object with its checks and derived diagram, the design specifications with the precision analysis and its re-solve at 0.95 assurance, the count script supplied to the data controller, and the literature sizing are deposited there, so the theory object, the design analysis and the literature sizing can be reproduced now. The outcome-model code will be written against simulated data, as described above, and deposited in the same location before the extract is transferred, together with the frozen feature inventory and the archived prior table. The four packages the protocol relies on are cited by their concept identifiers, and the releases in use are theoryforge 0.6.0 [@bernabeuTheoryforge2026], pilotr 0.3.0 [@bernabeuPilotr2026], scopusflow 0.4.0 [@bernabeuScopusflow2026] and depictr 0.3.0 [@bernabeuDepictr2026]. The session records deposited beside every output record the versions used. The design-analysis figures were composed with depictr, whose audit checks each panel for a floor on rendered type size and for separation in greyscale at the width the journal prints, and refuses to save a panel that fails.
